questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That there appeared to be enough courses I could use as substitutes for the obligatory courses at home, as well as it being placed in an interesting location.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: What brought it down from 10 is all the administrative problems I had regarding getting pre-approvals for courses. But it was definitely still worth going.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got some emails with useful information from the international office at the host university, office hours of a person you could go to if you had issues, and an introduction event held by volunteer students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Through the university it was easy, as you just had to choose on an online form in a first-come-first-served principle. However, there were many that didn't get the opportunity to be offered housing  as you needed to click a specific box very early and many missed it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There isn't really an 'on campus' in Milan, as the university is spread out through many small campuses, often kind of close to each other.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The dorm I stayed at (Campus Martinitt) was a bit far away from the center, but it helped that there was a direct bus going from right outside the dorm and straight to the center and university so it wasn't that big an issue. The main problem with the dorm was that there was only one big kitchen for all 300-400 students living there, which meant it very often got very crowded.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a bit chaotic to find out how to do it at first, but after that it was pretty easy.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You did it through their online platform where you could choose the ones you wanted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could write to the international office and they could help you

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is pretty simple, and you don't have to do it immediately - you can try out multiple classes and then decide which ones you like the most.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Mostly the level was fine. In one course 'Comparative Political Systems' however, it felt more like being taught the contents of the course book than actual comparative politics, which was really irritating.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: All the classes were much smaller than the normal classes, and felt like a mix of a lecture and classroom discussion. There was a much bigger focus on learning facts by heart than getting the bigger understanding of the subject.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Comparative Political Systems
European Economic and Monetary Law
Multi-level Legal System
Global Criminal Organizations
Workshop: Human Rights and the Ombudsman

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
One course I would recommend NOT taking is Global Criminal Organizations if the professor is Landolfi Francesco. He took an interesting course topic and made the class absolutely horrible by being both a really bad teacher and having a terrible attitude toward the students.

European Economic and Monetary Law, Workshop: Human Rights and the Ombudsman, and Multi-level Legal System were all fine.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Getting coffee was super cheap, however getting a cup of tea was often ridiculously expensive. Mostly the prices were fairly close to the Danish ones, though a bit cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't really hear of any. There are probably some, but they are not geared towards getting exchange students as members.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The local Erasmus Student Network group held a lot of events throughout the semester. However, for most of them you had to pay to participate.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Travel. Milan is a great base for day or weekend trips, and it is super easy to do!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Do go up on the roof of the Duomo, the view is beautiful. 
There are a lot of beautiful cities close by, my favourites for a weekend trip are Cinque Terre and Venice!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy, the biggest for me was what was considered normal 'eating times', but as you could cook yourself it wasn't really an issue.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Living in a dorm helped, especially as I had an Italian roommate, but generally it is pretty hard to do as you are mainly in an exchange student bubble with other exchange students. My best suggestion would be going to a lot of the Erasmus activities as they were hosted by Italians. Especially those regularly playing beach volley sounded like they got pretty close.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There wasn't really any.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That everyone were a bit more easygoing instead of just always hurrying from A to B. This also includes going out way more often, both for just a coffee or for dinner.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Enjoy and have fun! Yes, you do need to study some, but it is important to prioritize going out, traveling and just having fun and exploring the new place you are at.
Eat out a lot - it is Italy and the food *is* good. 
Be prepared for a lot of chaos and things that don't go the way you want them to, but in the end it is definitely worth going anyway.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not really

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: As cliché as it sounds, the friendships I've made.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was for sure getting pre-approvals for the obligatory courses at home that I had to find substitutes for. It was an issue even before I left, where I had to send course wishes back and forth many times in order to finally find some courses that would get approved as a substitute for 'Europæisk Politik'. Then, when I got to Milan, it turned out that those courses that were supposed to be held the semester I was there had been moved to the next semester. So then I had to frantically search for new courses that could be approved. In the end it was solved, but only after about three weeks after classes had already started. This was a giant stress factor.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
